blocks.body:
Sorting a drawer of socks into matching pairs, listing which cities have direct flights between them, saying that two integers "leave the same remainder when divided by 3", ranking tasks so that each one comes after the tasks it depends on: all of these are statements about collections of objects and about how pairs of objects are linked. Sets are the collections; relations are the links.

This page sets up that language. The two ideas worth carrying away are that an equivalence relation is the same thing as a way of cutting a set into pieces, and that a partial order is a consistent way of saying "comes before" when not every pair has to be comparable.

blocks.title: Sets and how to describe them
blocks.body:
A set is a collection of objects, called its elements; we write $x \in A$ for "$x$ is an element of $A$" and $x \notin A$ otherwise. A set is determined by its elements alone: order and repetition do not matter, so $\{1,2,3\}$, $\{3,1,2\}$ and $\{1,1,2,3\}$ are the same set. This principle (two sets are equal exactly when they have the same elements) is called extensionality.

There are two common ways to describe a set. Listing (roster notation): $\{2,3,5,7\}$. Set-builder notation: $\{n \in \mathbb{Z} : n > 0 \text{ and } n^2 < 50\}$, read "the set of integers $n$ such that $n>0$ and $n^2<50$", which is $\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}$. The empty set $\varnothing$ has no elements at all.

$A$ is a subset of $B$, written $A \subseteq B$, if every element of $A$ is an element of $B$. So $A = B$ exactly when $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$; this "two inclusions" pattern is the standard way to prove two sets equal. Note that $\varnothing \subseteq A$ for every set $A$, because there is no element of $\varnothing$ that could fail to lie in $A$.

The power set $\mathcal{P}(A)$ is the set of all subsets of $A$. If $A$ has $n$ elements then $\mathcal{P}(A)$ has $2^n$: to build a subset you decide, independently for each of the $n$ elements, whether it is in or out.

blocks.title: Set operations
De Morgan's laws
blocks.body:
For any subsets $A, B$ of a universe $U$,
$$(A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c, \qquad (A \cap B)^c = A^c \cup B^c.$$

blocks.title: Proof of the first law
blocks.body: For any $x \in U$: $x \in (A\cup B)^c$ means $x$ is not in $A \cup B$, which happens exactly when $x \notin A$ and $x \notin B$, that is when $x \in A^c \cap B^c$. Each step is an "exactly when", so this proves both inclusions at once. The second law follows by applying the first to $A^c$ and $B^c$ and taking complements.

blocks.title: Relations as sets of pairs
blocks.body:
A relation from $A$ to $B$ is simply a subset $R \subseteq A \times B$; we write $a \mathrel{R} b$ for $(a,b) \in R$. A relation on $A$ is a subset of $A \times A$. For example, on $A = \{1,2,3,4\}$ the relation "divides" is
$$\{(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(1,4),(2,2),(2,4),(3,3),(4,4)\}.$$

Since $A \times A$ has $n^2$ elements when $|A| = n$, there are $2^{n^2}$ relations on an $n$-element set. A function $f : A \to B$ (see [[functions]]) is the special kind of relation in which every $a \in A$ is related to exactly one $b$.

Finite relations can be drawn in two handy ways. As a matrix: rows and columns indexed by elements, with a 1 in position $(a,b)$ when $a \mathrel{R} b$. As a directed graph: a dot for each element and an arrow $a \to b$ for each related pair. More generally an $n$-ary relation is a subset of $A_1 \times \dots \times A_n$; a table in a database, where each row is a tuple (name, date of birth, city), is exactly this.

blocks.title: Properties of a relation on A
Closures
blocks.body: If a relation lacks a property, we can add the fewest pairs needed to get it. The reflexive closure of $R$ is $R \cup \{(a,a) : a \in A\}$; the symmetric closure is $R \cup \{(b,a) : (a,b) \in R\}$. The transitive closure $R^+$ is the smallest transitive relation containing $R$: $a \mathrel{R^+} b$ exactly when there is a chain $a = x_0 \mathrel{R} x_1 \mathrel{R} \cdots \mathrel{R} x_k = b$ with $k \ge 1$. In graph terms, $R^+$ records which dots can be reached from which by following arrows; on an $n$-element set chains of at most $n$ steps suffice. Computing reachability like this is a basic task in [[graph-algorithms]].

blocks.title: Equivalence relation, class, partition
blocks.body:
An equivalence relation on $A$ is a relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive; it is often written $\sim$. The equivalence class of $a$ is $[a] = \{x \in A : x \sim a\}$. A partition of $A$ is a collection of nonempty subsets of $A$ (the blocks) such that every element of $A$ lies in exactly one block.

An equivalence relation is a notion of "the same for present purposes": same remainder mod 3, same birthday, same shape.

blocks.title: Equivalence relations are partitions
blocks.body: If $\sim$ is an equivalence relation on $A$, its equivalence classes form a partition of $A$. Conversely, if $\Pi$ is a partition of $A$, the relation "$a \sim b$ if and only if $a$ and $b$ lie in the same block of $\Pi$" is an equivalence relation whose classes are exactly the blocks of $\Pi$. These two constructions undo each other.

Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation. Each class $[a]$ is nonempty because $a \in [a]$ by reflexivity, and this also shows every element lies in at least one class. It remains to see that two classes are either equal or disjoint. Suppose $c \in [a] \cap [b]$, so $c \sim a$ and $c \sim b$. By symmetry $a \sim c$, and by transitivity $a \sim b$. Now if $x \in [a]$ then $x \sim a$ and $a \sim b$, so $x \sim b$ and $x \in [b]$; thus $[a] \subseteq [b]$, and by the same argument with $a, b$ swapped, $[b] \subseteq [a]$. So overlapping classes coincide, and every element lies in exactly one class.

For the converse, "same block" is reflexive (each $a$ is in its own block), symmetric (the wording is symmetric) and transitive (if $a, b$ share a block and $b, c$ share a block, these blocks both contain $b$, so they are the same block, which contains $a$ and $c$). The class of $a$ is the block containing $a$. Finally, starting from $\sim$, forming classes, and then taking "same class" gives back $\sim$, since $a \sim b$ exactly when $a \in [b]$.

blocks.title: Partial order
blocks.body:
A partial order on $A$ is a relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, usually written $\preceq$; the pair $(A, \preceq)$ is a partially ordered set, or poset. Elements $a, b$ are comparable if $a \preceq b$ or $b \preceq a$. A total (linear) order is a partial order in which every two elements are comparable.

Examples: $\le$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is total; $\subseteq$ on $\mathcal{P}(A)$ and divisibility on the positive integers are partial but not total ($\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ are incomparable, and so are 2 and 3).

blocks.title: Pictures and vocabulary for posets
blocks.body:
A finite poset is drawn as a Hasse diagram: put $b$ above $a$ and join them with a line when $a \prec b$ and nothing lies strictly between them. Loops and shortcut lines are left out, since reflexivity and transitivity restore them.

In a poset, $m$ is maximal if no element lies strictly above it, and greatest if every element lies below it; minimal and least are defined dually. A greatest element is automatically maximal and unique, but a poset can have many maximal elements and no greatest one. A chain is a set of pairwise comparable elements; an antichain is a set of pairwise incomparable ones.

A total order in which every nonempty subset has a least element is a well-order. The usual order on $\mathbb{N}$ is a well-order, and that fact is the engine behind [[induction]]; the usual order on $\mathbb{Z}$ is not (there is no least integer). Well-orders are studied in [[ordinals-cardinals]].

Every finite poset can be extended to a total order by repeatedly removing a minimal element and listing it next (a topological sort).

blocks.title: A glimpse further: why we are careful
blocks.body: It is tempting to allow any description to define a set. Russell's paradox shows the danger: if $R = \{x : x \notin x\}$ were a set, then $R \in R$ would hold exactly when $R \notin R$, a contradiction. Axiomatic set theory (the Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms) avoids this by only allowing set-builder notation inside a set already known to exist, as in $\{x \in A : \dots\}$. University readers will also meet Zorn's lemma (a nonempty poset in which every chain has an upper bound has a maximal element), which is equivalent to the axiom of choice.

blocks.title: A transitive closure
blocks.body: On $A = \{1,2,3,4\}$ let $R = \{(1,2),(2,3),(3,4)\}$. Which of the four properties does $R$ have? Find its transitive closure.
blocks.solution:
$R$ is not reflexive (no $(1,1)$), not symmetric ($(1,2) \in R$ but $(2,1) \notin R$), and it is antisymmetric, since there are no two distinct elements related both ways. It is not transitive: $(1,2), (2,3) \in R$ but $(1,3) \notin R$.

Chains of arrows: $1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4$. Two-step chains give $(1,3), (2,4)$, and the three-step chain gives $(1,4)$. So
$$R^+ = \{(1,2),(1,3),(1,4),(2,3),(2,4),(3,4)\},$$
which is exactly the strict order $<$ on $\{1,2,3,4\}$. Adding the four pairs $(a,a)$ turns it into the partial (indeed total) order $\le$.

blocks.title: Counting equivalence relations
blocks.body: How many equivalence relations are there on $\{1,2,3,4\}$?

blocks.title: Chains and antichains under divisibility
blocks.body: Order $\{1,2,\dots,12\}$ by divisibility. Find its minimal and maximal elements and an antichain of size 6. Then show that any 7 of these numbers include two, one of which divides the other.
blocks.solution:
The only minimal element is 1, which divides everything, so it is in fact least. An element is maximal if none of its multiples other than itself lies in the set, that is, if $2m > 12$: the maximal elements are $7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12$. No one of these divides another (the smallest proper multiple of each exceeds 12), so they form an antichain of size 6.

Now take any 7 numbers from 1 to 12. Write each as $2^k m$ with $m$ odd. The odd part $m$ is one of $1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11$: only 6 possibilities. By the [[pigeonhole]] principle two of the chosen numbers, say $2^j m$ and $2^k m$ with $j < k$, have the same odd part, and then the first divides the second. So 6 is the largest size of an antichain here. The same argument shows that among any $n+1$ numbers from $\{1, \dots, 2n\}$ one divides another.

blocks.body:
- $\in$ and $\subseteq$ are different: $1 \in \{1,2\}$ and $\{1\} \subseteq \{1,2\}$, but $\{1\} \notin \{1,2\}$.
- $\varnothing$ and $\{\varnothing\}$ differ: the first has no elements, the second has one.
- Antisymmetric does not mean "not symmetric". The equality relation is both symmetric and antisymmetric; the relation $\{(1,2),(2,1),(1,3)\}$ on $\{1,2,3\}$ is neither.
- A common false proof claims symmetry and transitivity imply reflexivity ("from $a R b$ get $b R a$, then $a R a$"). It only works for elements related to something. The empty relation on a nonempty set is symmetric and transitive but not reflexive.
- Maximal is not the same as greatest: in the divisibility example there are six maximal elements and no greatest one.

This vocabulary is the setting for [[proof-methods]], where "prove two sets equal" and "prove a relation is an equivalence" are standard exercises. Congruence modulo $n$ is an equivalence relation whose classes are the residue classes of [[congruences]], and quotient constructions throughout algebra (cosets in [[groups]], for instance) are partitions by an equivalence relation. In [[automata]], the states of a minimal automaton correspond to the classes of a natural equivalence relation on strings. Comparing the sizes of infinite sets, and extending induction beyond $\mathbb{N}$ with well-orders, is the subject of [[ordinals-cardinals]]. Counting subsets and relations leads into [[counting]].

1. Prove that $A \setminus (B \cup C) = (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C)$ by showing both inclusions.
2. On $\mathbb{Z}$, define $a \sim b$ when $a - b$ is divisible by 5. Prove that $\sim$ is an equivalence relation and list its classes.
3. How many relations on a 3-element set are reflexive? How many are symmetric?
4. Draw the Hasse diagram of the divisors of 30 under divisibility. Is there a greatest element?
